items.text: "Sales to marketing" gets treated online like one door.
Do not walk into this switch thinking you are starting from zero.

blocks.heading: Sales Already Gives You (the Real Overlap)

items.text: You have sat across from real customers and heard the objection behind the objection, the actual reason someone hesitates, not the polite reason they say out loud.

Marketing is persuasion at scale instead of one-to-one, but the underlying skill, building a case, anticipating pushback, and closing with a clear next step, transfers directly into campaign copy, pitch decks, and stakeholder buy-in for a marketing plan.

blocks.heading: Skill Stack to Build Before You Apply

items.text: Do not try to build all four lanes' worth of skill at once.
One case study or customer story, one campaign or pitch email, one one-pager or battlecard.
Google Digital Garage, Meta Blueprint, and HubSpot Academy all offer free, credible certifications in a few hours to a few days.
Do not resign, enrol in an expensive marketing course, or announce the switch to your whole team before you have tested your fit properly.
Pick one lane from the four above based on your honest overlap-and-gap read.
Start volunteering for one visible marketing-adjacent task inside your current role, even informally.

blocks.heading: Marketing Actually Needs That Sales Doesn't Teach

items.text: Sales persuasion happens live, adjusted in real time to one person's reaction.
This means practising structured writing: a one-pager, a case study, a short campaign email, written to be understood in one read with no follow-up question allowed.
Start by doing one small piece of marketing-adjacent work inside your current role: write a case study, build a battlecard, support a product launch with sales-side input.
Connect the ask to what your manager already cares about, pipeline quality, deal velocity, customer retention, not to your own boredom with sales.
Ask for a specific, bounded next step: a trial project, a shadow arrangement with the marketing team, or a formal transfer conversation, rather than a vague "can I move to marketing."
Your existing relationships and track record are your biggest asset here, you do not need a stranger-proof portfolio; you need a manager who has already seen you deliver.
Sales pay is commonly split between a fixed base and uncapped or high-ceiling variable commission tied to closed deals.
Marketing pay tends to be steadier month to month.
Compare your realistic average annual earning across a normal year in sales, not your best quarter, against the marketing offer, for an honest comparison.
Applying to marketing roles with a resume still written entirely in sales-quota language, with no marketing-relevant framing.
Enrolling in a long, expensive marketing course before writing a single real content piece or testing whether you actually enjoy the work.
Targeting "marketing" broadly instead of picking one lane that matches your actual sales background and strengths.
Comparing your best sales-commission month to a marketing base salary and concluding the switch "doesn't pay."
Waiting for a formal internal opening instead of starting visible marketing-adjacent work now, inside your current role.
